batchName: Empire: Diocletian and Constantine (AD 284-337) - Easy Batch 1

questions.question: What did Diocletian's Edict on Maximum Prices of 301 try to do?
options: Replace silver coins with new gold ones
Fix soldiers' wages for their lifetimes
Set top prices for over a thousand goods
Abolish all taxes on Italian land
questions.explanation: The edict blamed greedy merchants for inflation and capped the prices of more than a thousand goods. It ignored supply and demand, and goods slipped into a black market.
questions.sourceQuote: In late 301 his Edict on Maximum Prices (*Edictum de Pretiis Rerum Venalium*) blamed greedy merchants and set top prices for more than a thousand goods.

questions.question: In which Roman province was Diocletian born?
questions.explanation: Diocletian was born around AD 243 in Dalmatia, on the Adriatic coast of modern Croatia. His family was humble, and ancient writers called his father either a scribe or a freed slave.
questions.sourceQuote: Diocletian, the soldier-emperor who pulled Rome back from the brink, was born around AD 243 in Dalmatia, a Roman province on the Adriatic coast of modern Croatia.

questions.question: What does the word 'Tetrarchy' mean?
questions.explanation: The Tetrarchy comes from a Greek word meaning 'rule by four': two senior emperors and two junior Caesars. When the senior pair retired, the Caesars were supposed to step up.
questions.sourceQuote: This arrangement is called the Tetrarchy, from a Greek word meaning “rule by four”.

questions.question: When begged to return to power, Diocletian said no one would ask if they could see what?
questions.explanation: Diocletian said that anyone who saw the cabbages he had grown with his own hands would never ask him to come back. He made the reply at Carnuntum in 308.
questions.sourceQuote: If they could see the cabbages he had planted with his own hands, he replied, they would never ask.

questions.question: In which year did Constantine go to war with Maxentius and fight at the Milvian Bridge?
questions.explanation: By 312 Constantine and his brother-in-law Maxentius, ruler of Rome, were at war. The decisive battle came on 28 October that year.
questions.sourceQuote: By 312 Constantine and his brother-in-law Maxentius, ruler of Rome, were at war.

questions.question: Where did the troops proclaim Constantine Augustus after his father's death in 306?
questions.explanation: Constantine's father died at York on 25 July 306, and the army there proclaimed Constantine Augustus. Galerius grudgingly recognised him only as Caesar.
questions.sourceQuote: He joined his father, and when his father died at York on 25 July 306, the troops proclaimed Constantine Augustus.

questions.question: Which Greek city did Constantine refound as Constantinople?
questions.explanation: Constantine refounded Byzantium on the strait between Europe and Asia and dedicated it in 330 as Constantinople. It remained a capital for more than a thousand years.
questions.sourceQuote: He refounded Byzantium, a Greek city on the strait between Europe and Asia, dedicating it in 330 as Constantinople, “Constantine's City”.

questions.question: Roughly how many provinces did the empire have after Diocletian's reforms?
questions.explanation: Diocletian doubled the provinces from about fifty to almost a hundred. Smaller provinces meant no governor held enough land or soldiers to rebel.
questions.sourceQuote: He doubled the provinces, from about fifty to almost a hundred, so that no governor held enough land or soldiers to rebel.

questions.question: Which empire, ruled by the Sasanian kings, was Rome's gravest threat in the East?
questions.explanation: Persia under the Sasanian kings was Rome's great eastern rival. In 297 the Persians crushed Galerius in northern Mesopotamia.
questions.sourceQuote: The gravest threat was Persia, ruled by the Sasanian kings, Rome's great eastern rival.

questions.question: What did the Edict of Milan of 313 grant?
options: Pardons to all exiled pagan priests
Freedom of worship to all religions
Tax exemption to all Christian clergy
questions.explanation: The Edict of Milan granted freedom of worship to all religions. It also returned property that had been seized from Christians.
questions.sourceQuote: In 313 Constantine and his eastern co-emperor, Licinius, agreed the Edict of Milan, granting freedom of worship to all religions and returning property seized from Christians.
